passage:
Vijay had one night left. The principal’s meeting was at nine the next morning, and his petition to ban plastic bottles in the canteen needed forty more signatures. He and Ganga stood in the corridor with clipboards.
A classmate, Ruchi, said, “I’d sign, but the refill station has been broken for weeks. Where will we get water?”
“That’s an excuse,” said Vijay. “You’re part of the problem.”
Ruchi’s smile vanished. Ganga said softly, “She’s asking a real question.”
Vijay’s ears grew hot. He wanted to argue, but he took a breath and said, “Okay. Let’s add the station to the petition.”

qa.q: When was the principal's meeting?
qa.a: The principal's meeting was at nine the next morning.

qa.q: What was Vijay feeling when he called Ruchi part of the problem?
qa.a: He was passionate and certain, under time pressure. In his mind anyone who disagreed was blocking the cause.

qa.q: What turning point helped Vijay change course?
qa.a: Ganga pointed out that Ruchi was asking a real question. Vijay took a breath and added the broken refill station to the petition.

qa.q: How might Ruchi have felt when Vijay called her part of the problem?
qa.a: Ruchi probably felt stung and unfairly blamed, since her smile vanished. She had raised a practical concern, not refused to help.

grounding: Shows a teenager passionate about a first campaign and certain that anyone who disagrees is wrong, then pausing to listen.

passage:
The lane behind Afreen’s building had no streetlight, and she was tired of walking home in the dark. She and five friends went door to door with a petition. By Saturday they had twenty-six signatures, and Afreen felt part of something big.
Mr. Bhatt on the ground floor refused to sign. “The society funds are low,” he said.
“He just doesn’t care about safety,” Afreen muttered.
Saurabh, one of the group, said, “Maybe he’s worried about the cost. Maybe we should ask how much.”
Afreen frowned, then knocked on Mr. Bhatt’s door again. “Can we show you the price?” she asked.

qa.q: How many signatures did the group have by Saturday?
qa.a: They had twenty-six signatures by Saturday.

qa.q: What was Afreen feeling as she muttered about Mr. Bhatt?
qa.a: She was frustrated and sure that he was wrong, and she felt the cause was a matter of safety. Her belonging to the group made disagreement feel like carelessness.

qa.q: What changed when Afreen went back to Mr. Bhatt's door?
qa.a: She stopped assuming he did not care and offered to show him the price. That gave him a chance to say what worried him.

qa.q: How might Saurabh have seen Mr. Bhatt's refusal differently from Afreen?
qa.a: Saurabh saw a possible money worry rather than carelessness. Saurabh asked how much it would cost, which shows a search for the reason behind the refusal.

grounding: Shows a teenager passionate about a local campaign who first assumes those who disagree are wrong, then listens.

passage:
Dear Varun,
Guess what? I've joined Save Chandni Lake. The municipality plans to build a car park on half of the lake, and our group of thirty teenagers is fighting it. We make posters every Saturday, we've collected nine hundred signatures, and last week the local paper printed our photo! I've never felt so alive. These are my people.
Yesterday my neighbour, Mr Kaul, said the car park might help the hospital nearby, since ambulances get stuck. I told him he obviously doesn't care about nature. He looked hurt. Now I'm not sure I was fair. Is it possible to be completely right and still miss something?
Write back.
Zubin

qa.q: How many signatures has the group collected?
qa.a: Nine hundred.

qa.q: How does Zubin feel about the campaign group?
qa.a: Passionate and alive, with a strong sense of belonging, calling them 'my people'.

qa.q: What could Zubin do after the talk with Mr Kaul?
qa.a: Apologise, ask more about the ambulance problem, and bring it to the group to see if a plan can protect both the lake and hospital access.

qa.q: How might Mr Kaul have felt when Zubin said he didn't care about nature?
qa.a: Hurt and misunderstood, since he was worried about ambulances getting stuck.

grounding: A teenager finds passion and belonging in a local campaign and begins to notice the pull to dismiss anyone who disagrees.

passage: Hafsa, you want to know how I got into campaigning? Okay, it's Farida, Class 11, and it started with the school's rule that girls must wear skirts, even in winter. A few of us started a petition for trousers as an option. Within a week, a hundred and forty students had signed, and we had a group chat called Trouser Revolution. I've never felt so part of something. We had badges! But here's the embarrassing bit. When my friend Nazneen said she liked the skirts and didn't want to sign, I told her she was 'part of the problem'. She stopped sitting with me. We won the trouser option in February. Nazneen still wears the skirt, and that's completely fine. I just wish I hadn't said that.

qa.q: What was the group chat called?
qa.a: Trouser Revolution.

qa.q: How does Farida feel now about what was said to Nazneen?
qa.a: Farida feels regretful and embarrassed, wishing the words 'part of the problem' had never been said.

qa.q: What could Farida do to repair things with Nazneen?
qa.a: Apologise directly and tell Nazneen that wearing the skirt is fine, since the campaign was about having an option.

qa.q: How might Nazneen have felt being called 'part of the problem'?
qa.a: Hurt and judged for simply liking the skirt, which is why she stopped sitting with Farida.

grounding: A teenager feels passion and belonging in a school campaign, and also a certainty that led her to dismiss a friend who disagreed.

passage: Monday: Charu joined the eco club's campaign to ban plastic straws and cups from the school canteen. At the first meeting, twenty students cheered every idea, and Charu felt she had found her place. Wednesday: she marched to the canteen with Ojas and told Raju uncle, the canteen owner, that he was 'killing the planet'. Raju uncle said steel cups cost more and got stolen. Charu rolled her eyes. 'Excuses.' Ojas said nothing. The next Friday: Ojas showed the club a list: steel cups from the wholesale market, the cost for a term, and an idea for a deposit so the cups came back. Raju uncle agreed to try it. Charu felt proud of the club, and a bit ashamed of 'excuses'. She went back to the canteen and said sorry.

qa.q: What did Raju uncle say about steel cups?
qa.a: That they cost more and got stolen.

qa.q: How did Charu feel at the end of the week?
qa.a: Proud of the club, and a bit ashamed of dismissing Raju uncle's concerns as 'excuses'.

qa.q: What did Ojas do that actually solved the problem?
qa.a: Took Raju uncle's worries seriously and researched steel cups, costs and a deposit idea, so he could agree.

qa.q: How might Raju uncle have felt when Charu said he was 'killing the planet'?
qa.a: Accused and defensive, since he had real worries about cost and theft.

grounding: Over a week a teenager feels the passion and belonging of a first cause, and learns that those who disagree may have real reasons.

subtype: First cause a teenager cares about [Actor]
passage: Dhruv, you're sixteen and on fire about the lake? Good. Let your Ojas Mama tell you about my lake. At fifteen, in Bhopal, I joined a group of students trying to stop the lake edge being filled for a car park. Oh, the feeling! Banners, meetings in someone's garage, songs we wrote ourselves. For the first time I belonged to something bigger than my marks. And I was so sure. Anyone who disagreed was a villain. When our neighbour Mr Qureshi said the car park would help his little shop, I called him greedy to his face. He just looked at me, tired. Years later I learnt that shop was all that fed his family. We did save half the lake, you know. I'm still proud of that. But I wish I'd asked him one question before I judged him.

qa.q: What was the lake edge going to be filled for?
qa.a: For a car park.

qa.q: How did young Ojas feel about the campaign?
qa.a: He felt passionate and proud, belonging to something bigger than his marks, and completely sure he was right.

qa.q: What choice in the story does Ojas regret, and what would have been better?
qa.a: Calling Mr Qureshi greedy to his face; asking one question about the shop first would have kept the cause without judging a struggling neighbour.

qa.q: How might Mr Qureshi have felt when he was called greedy?
qa.a: He probably felt tired and hurt, misjudged by a teenager who didn't know the shop fed his family.

grounding: Ojas Mama recalls his first cause as a teenager: the passion and belonging, and the certainty that everyone who disagreed was wrong.
